chapter: Local 94, Local 808 and the union convention
title: Weak unions in small towns, and Marvin Young the lawyer and arranger
summary: Love and Fields agree unions are weak outside the big cities; Fields tells how he gave Marvin Young an arrangement and Young became a fine arranger.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: You mentioned earlier that the union has been weakened lately; it certainly has, at this level, your smaller towns; not in Los Angeles and New York, big cities where you have studio work they're strong, but in these little towns like here the unions are terrible.
Definitely so, and really, believe it or not Preston, it's a little weak, I think, even in the larger towns. We have a black secretary out there, Marvin Young,--

I'll tell you about a coincidence--you know, he's a fine musician too--and when he was in Chicago, before he went, he's hard working and very clever, you know, he's an attorney, but when he was in Chicago, some kind of way--what's that club, Club DeLisa?

I think I was playing there once and got acquainted with him, he had an act or something and I did a number and I kind of liked it, and at that time I spoke to him and told him I liked it. He said do you want it? I said I would like to have this arrangement and he said I'll bring you one. I said what do I owe you; just tell them where you got him, let me do some arranging and he did become a very nice arranger.
Well you know, Marv was the music director for a time for the Lucy Show.
Yeah. And another well known musician, a brass man, a trombone man and writer, J.J. Johnson. He finally got straightened.
